clinicalPearls: Profuse watery rhinorrhoea triggered soon after eating, especially hot and spicy foods
It is a form of non-allergic rhinitis mediated by cholinergic reflexes rather than by allergy
Symptoms are predominantly clear nasal discharge without significant itch, sneezing or nasal blockage
It is more common in older adults and can be socially troublesome
There is no association with specific food allergy, and allergy testing is typically unnecessary
Pre-meal use of a topical anticholinergic nasal spray is effective for many patients
reference.pathophysiology: Gustatory rhinitis results from a vagally mediated cholinergic reflex in which the act of eating, particularly spicy or hot food, stimulates nasal glandular secretion. Afferent signals from the upper aerodigestive tract provoke parasympathetic efferent activity to the nasal mucosa, driving watery hypersecretion without an allergic or inflammatory basis. Because the mechanism is cholinergic, topical antimuscarinic therapy blocks the glandular response and controls the rhinorrhoea.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the clear temporal link to eating
Distinguishing it from allergic rhinitis by history and, if needed, allergy testing
Exclusion of cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhoea when discharge is persistent or unilateral
Nasal examination to exclude structural or inflammatory disease
Review of medications contributing to rhinitis
redFlags: Unilateral clear discharge raising concern for cerebrospinal fluid leak
Associated bleeding, crusting or a mass
Failure to respond to appropriate anticholinergic therapy
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and readily controlled with pre-meal anticholinergic nasal spray and dietary awareness, though it tends to persist without treatment.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as food allergy and ordering unnecessary tests
Overlooking a cerebrospinal fluid leak when discharge is unilateral
Failing to offer effective topical anticholinergic treatment
Confusing it with other non-allergic rhinitis subtypes
management: Use a pre-meal topical intranasal anticholinergic spray such as ipratropium bromide to block the cholinergic glandular reflex
Advise avoidance or limitation of trigger foods, particularly hot and spicy meals
Reassure the patient that the condition is benign and non-allergic, so allergy testing is generally unnecessary
Review and rationalise medications that may be contributing to rhinitis
Exclude cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhoea when the discharge is persistent or unilateral
Refer to otolaryngology or allergy services if symptoms are refractory or the diagnosis is uncertain
